subject: mathematics_1b
question_text: Find the equation of the straight line passing through the point (1, 2) and making an angle of 60° with the line √3x + y + 2 = 0.

verification.note: Source: Sri Chaitanya, FAST TRACK IPE for Jr. Students — Mathematics-IB (2026-27 edition), book p.156, chapter 3 THE STRAIGHT LINE, Long Answer question 12(ii). **Only the question was taken. The solution, the step order and the mark split are this answer book's own work** — see docs/ORIGINALITY_MATHS.md. THE MARK SPLIT IS OURS, NOT THE BOOK'S: the volume prints a chapter-level marks banner over this section but no per-step allocation on any answer. The split rewards the angle condition and the two branches it opens: two marks for writing tan 60° = |(m − m₁)/(1 + m m₁)|, two for opening the modulus and two for solving both branches, with one each for the given slope and the final lines. This book prints almost no exam-appearance years, so appearances[] is empty — the chapter has long been examined, we simply have no sourced years for this question. Paper position: Maths-1B Section C prints 3 long answer questions at 8 marks each and the student answers any 2, under the 2026-27 pattern. This is a coaching publication, not a TSBIE document, so the split stays unverified until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. Both answers were substituted back. y − 2 = 0 passes through (1, 2) and its slope 0 gives tan θ = |(−√3 − 0)/(1 + 0)| = √3; √3x − y + 2 − √3 = 0 gives √3 − 2 + 2 − √3 = 0 at (1, 2) and its slope √3 gives tan θ = |(−√3 − √3)/(1 − 3)| = √3. A second check by inclination: the given line has slope −√3, so its inclination is 120°; turning 60° each way gives 60° and 180°, whose tangents are √3 and 0 — the same two slopes. STEM AS PRINTED: the book asks for the equation of the straight line, in the singular. Two lines through (1, 2) make 60° with the given line, one turned each way, and both are genuine answers — a 60° turn from an inclination of 120° reaches 60° and 180°. The card answers the sensible reading and reports both, and says so in the working rather than silently choosing one.

recall_prompt: Say how you would solve this — name the angle formula, and say why this question really has two answers.

steps.label: Slope of the given line
steps.margin_note: First mark. Read the slope as −a/b. Here a = √3 and b = 1, so the slope is negative.

steps.memory_tip: Slope is −a/b. With b = 1 the slope is just minus the coefficient of x.

steps.label: Write the 60° condition
steps.margin_note: Two marks. Write the angle formula in full, then substitute m₁ = −√3 and tan 60° = √3, watching the sign in the denominator.

steps.why: tan 60° = √3 turns the angle statement into an equation with only m in it, and the surd stays exact all the way through.
common_mistakes: Using sin 60° or cos 60° in place of tan 60°.
Writing 1 + m m₁ as 1 + √3 m, losing the sign of m₁.
steps.memory_tip: tan θ = |(m − m₁)/(1 + m m₁)| with m₁ = −√3, so the denominator becomes 1 − √3 m, not 1 + √3 m.

steps.label: Open the modulus
steps.margin_note: Two marks. Clear the fraction, then remove the modulus as ±. Both signs are kept — the question has two answers.
lines: A 60° turn can be made either way from the
given line, so both signs give a real line.

steps.why: There are two lines through a point at 60° to a given line, one turned each way, so both branches are kept even though the question says line in the singular.

Multiplying only one side by √3 when the modulus is cleared.
steps.memory_tip: Two lines at 60°: one turned each way. Keep both signs even when the question says the line.

steps.label: Solve both branches
steps.margin_note: Two marks. Multiply out the √3 bracket first — √3 × √3 m is 3m — then collect. m = 0 is a genuine answer, not an error.

recall.must_convey: That the two branches give m = 0 and m = √3.

steps.why: Note that √3 × √3 m = 3m, which is what makes both branches collapse to simple linear equations with no surd left in m.

Rejecting m = 0 as impossible; it is the horizontal line y = 2.
steps.memory_tip: √3 × √3 = 3, so the surd clears itself. m = 0 is a real answer: it is the horizontal line.

steps.label: Write both lines
steps.margin_note: The last mark. Put each slope into y − y₁ = m(x − x₁) at (1, 2). Expand √3(x − 1) as √3x − √3.
